# Programmable computer (stored program) (`programmable_computer`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/computing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Computing, control & information theory (`computing`)
- Deps: needs algorithm_concept; helped by binary_numbers, logic_gates_switching, punched_card_control, mechanical_calculator, vacuum_tube, computer_memory, turing_machine_computability, semiconductors_transistor
- Core idea: A general computer has five parts: an arithmetic unit, a memory of numbered cells, a control unit, input and output. The work is laid down as a program, a list of very simple instructions such as 'add the number in cell 17 to the accumulator' or 'store the result in cell 40', which the control unit fetches and carries out one after another. A useful control instruction is the conditional jump: 'if the result is negative, continue at instruction 12', which allows decisions and loops. In a stored-program design, instructions are themselves encoded in memory, so a new task needs only a new program, not rewiring, and programs can be loaded, altered and produced by other programs.
- Pitfalls:
  - Describing a fast calculator; the essence is automatic sequencing with conditional branching, not speed of arithmetic
  - Programming by plugboards and switches as on ENIAC, where each new problem took days of rewiring
  - Assuming a programmable machine must use binary. ENIAC counted in decimal, and the Analytical Engine design used decimal wheels
  - Underestimating memory and reliability: the logic was within reach in 1945, a memory of a few thousand reliable binary digits was the real obstacle
  - Naming one inventor: Babbage, Zuse, Atanasoff, Turing, Eckert and Mauchly, von Neumann, Williams and Kilburn, and Wilkes each have a real but partial claim
- History: islamic: 9th c. – the Banu Musa's flute player with a pinned cylinder; 1206 al-Jazari's automata with peg drums, early machines whose sequence can be changed; europe: 1834–1837 – Babbage designs the Analytical Engine with store, mill, cards and conditional branching (never built); 1843 Lovelace's notes; 1936 Turing's universal machine; 1941 Zuse's Z3, a program-controlled relay computer (Berlin); 1943–1944 Colossus, electronic and special-purpose (Bletchley Park); June 1948 Manchester 'Baby' runs the first stored program; 1949 EDSAC in regular use (Cambridge); americas: 1939–1942 – Atanasoff and Berry's electronic equation solver (not programmable); 1944 Harvard Mark I; 1945–1946 ENIAC; 1945 von Neumann's First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC sets out the stored-program design (the share of Eckert and Mauchly is disputed); 1951 UNIVAC I
- Read:
  - L. F. Menabrea & Ada Lovelace, Sketch of the Analytical Engine Invented by Charles Babbage, Scientific Memoirs 3 (1843)
  - John von Neumann, First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC (1945)
  - Martin Campbell-Kelly & William Aspray, Computer: A History of the Information Machine (1996)
